questions.explanation: A proton-rich (neutron-deficient) nucleus seeks stability by converting excess protons into neutrons. This is accomplished through two competing processes: electron capture, in which an inner orbital electron is absorbed by the nucleus converting a proton to a neutron; or beta-plus decay, in which a positron is emitted achieving the same result. Alpha decay is possible in heavy proton-rich nuclei but is not the primary expected mode. Beta-minus decay is the characteristic decay of neutron-rich nuclei and would worsen the proton excess rather than correct it.

questions.explanation: The hematopoietic (bone marrow) system is the most radiosensitive organ system in the human body. The gastrointestinal system is next in sensitivity, while the central nervous system, muscle, and skeletal systems are far more radioresistant.

This distance corresponds to only a few cell diameters, which is why external alpha radiation cannot penetrate skin but is extremely hazardous if inhaled or ingested.

Bremsstrahlung production increases with electron kinetic energy and with the atomic number Z of the absorber (∝ Z²). Photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, and pair production are photon interaction mechanisms, not relevant to charged particle directly.

variants: Which neutron interaction is most important for slowing down neutrons to thermal energies?

questions.explanation: Elastic scattering (billiard-ball type, conserving kinetic energy) is the dominant mechanism for neutron moderation. Maximum energy transfer per collision occurs when the target nucleus mass equals the neutron mass, hence hydrogen (proton) is the ideal moderator. The average energy loss per elastic collision is: $$ \bar{\Delta E} = \frac{2A}{(1+A)^2} E_n $$ where A is the mass number of the target. Inelastic scattering can also slow neutrons but requires a threshold energy and is less important at low energies. Radiative capture and fission remove neutrons from the population rather than moderate them.

At **3.5–4.5 rad**, no detectable clinical effects occur. At **35–45 rad**, subclinical hematopoietic depression may appear but mortality is negligible. At **100–200 rad**, ARS begins and mortality is very low, this marks the lower threshold of the hematopoietic syndrome. At **3,500–4,500 rad**, the gastrointestinal syndrome dominates with death in days. At **35,000–45,000 rad**, the cerebrovascular/CNS syndrome causes death within hours. With modern medical support, the survivable dose may extend to ~6 Gy.

questions.explanation: In the diagnostic and therapeutic energy range of ~0.1–10 MeV for low-Z materials such as soft tissue (effective Z ≈ 7.5), **Compton scattering** dominates. At 1 MeV: the photoelectric effect is negligible (cross-section ∝ Z³/E³, very small at this energy); pair production requires a threshold of 1.022 MeV and becomes significant only above ~5–10 MeV in tissue; coherent scattering is negligible above ~0.1 MeV; photonuclear reactions require energies >5–10 MeV. Bremsstrahlung is an electron, not photon, interaction. Compton scattering dominates from roughly 0.1 MeV to several MeV in tissue.

variants: Which of the following types of decay "competes" with positron decay?

questions.explanation: Both positron (β⁺) decay and electron capture (EC) are competing processes that reduce the atomic number Z by 1 while leaving mass number A unchanged, effectively converting a proton into a neutron: $$ p \rightarrow n + e^+ + \nu_e \quad (\beta^+) $$ $$ p + e^- \rightarrow n + \nu_e \quad (EC) $$ β⁺ decay requires a minimum Q-value of **1.022 MeV** (to produce the positron mass × 2). When Q < 1.022 MeV, only EC can occur; when Q > 1.022 MeV, both compete. Higher Z nuclei favor EC because inner-shell electrons are closer to the nucleus. Internal conversion competes with gamma emission, not β⁺. Auger electrons follow EC or IC but are not competing decay modes themselves.

questions.explanation: The three fundamental physical methods for external radiation protection are: (1) **Time** , minimizing exposure duration reduces dose proportionally (D ∝ t); (2) **Distance** , increasing distance reduces dose following the inverse-square law $$ D \propto \frac{1}{r^2} $$; (3) **Shielding** , interposing attenuating material reduces intensity exponentially $$ I = I_0 e^{-\mu x} $$. Protective clothing guards against contamination, not external penetrating radiation. Whole-body counting and bioassay monitor **internal** contamination.

**Note on Units:** While mathematically 0.005 μCi equals 11,100 dpm, the unit **'dpm/100 cm²'** is strictly used for **surface contamination limits**, not sealed source leak tests. Ranking by these parameters: **Lead** (Pb, Z = 82, ρ = 11.3 g/cm³) is the most effective; **Iron** (Fe, Z = 26, ρ = 7.87 g/cm³) is next; **Concrete** (effective Z ≈ 14, ρ ≈ 2.3 g/cm³) follows; **Water** (H₂O, effective Z ≈ 3.3, ρ = 1.0 g/cm³) is least effective per unit thickness. The distractor **Pb > Al > H₂O > Fe** is wrong because aluminum (Al, Z = 13, ρ = 2.7 g/cm³) is less effective than iron and is not a standard gamma shield. Note that water and concrete are excellent neutron moderators due to hydrogen content, but for gamma attenuation per unit thickness the correct descending order is: Pb > Fe > Concrete > H₂O.

variants: If a shielding material has a half-value layer of 0.5 inches and a buildup factor of 2, how much shielding is required to reduce the exposure rate from 200 mR/hr to 50 mR/hr?

Given a buildup factor of 2 and a half-value layer of 0.5 inches, what shielding thickness reduces an exposure rate from 200 mR/hr to 50 mR/hr?
questions.explanation:
With a buildup factor B, the transmitted exposure rate is given by:

$$I = I_0 \times B \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$

where n is the number of HVLs. Setting I = 50 mR/hr, I₀ = 200 mR/hr, and B = 2:

$$50 = 200 \times 2 \times \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n$$

$$\frac{50}{400} = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n \Rightarrow n = 3 \text{ HVLs}$$

Thickness = 3 × 0.5 in = **1.5 inches**.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**
- **0.5 inches (1 HVL):** Yields I = 200 × 2 × 0.5 = 200 mR/hr , no net reduction due to buildup.
- **1.0 inches (2 HVLs):** Correct only if the buildup factor is ignored (200 × (1/4) = 50 mR/hr without B), reflecting a common error of omitting B.
- **2.0 inches (4 HVLs):** Overcorrects; yields 200 × 2 × (1/16) = 25 mR/hr.
- **2.5 inches (5 HVLs):** Yields 200 × 2 × (1/32) ≈ 12.5 mR/hr , excessive.
- **3.0 inches (6 HVLs):** Severe overestimate; yields 200 × 2 × (1/64) ≈ 6.25 mR/hr.

Reference: Bushberg et al., *The Essential Physics of Medical Imaging*, 3rd ed., Ch. 3; NCRP Report No. 49.

variants: The units used to express μ/ρ (the mass attenuation coefficient) are:
What are the correct SI-derived units for the mass attenuation coefficient μ/ρ?

questions.explanation:
The **linear attenuation coefficient** μ has units of cm⁻¹ (or 1/cm). Dividing by mass density ρ (units: g/cm³) gives the **mass attenuation coefficient**:

$$\frac{\mu}{\rho} = \frac{\text{cm}^{-1}}{\text{g/cm}^3} = \frac{\text{cm}^{-1} \times \text{cm}^3}{\text{g}} = \frac{\text{cm}^2}{\text{g}}$$

This quantity is material-dependent but density-independent, making it useful for comparing attenuation across materials of different physical states.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**
- **1/cm (cm⁻¹):** Units of the linear attenuation coefficient μ itself, not μ/ρ.
- **g/cm²:** Inverted unit , this is areal density (mass per unit area), a separate quantity used in shielding calculations.
- **g/cm³:** Units of density ρ alone, not the ratio μ/ρ.
- **cm³/g:** Results from incorrectly cubing rather than squaring the length dimension , a common algebraic error.
- **cm/g:** Arises if μ is incorrectly assigned units of cm⁻² instead of cm⁻¹, yielding one too few powers of cm.

Reference: ICRU Report 33; Bushberg et al., *The Essential Physics of Medical Imaging*, 3rd ed., Ch. 3.

variants: A photon beam is reduced to 0.1 of its initial intensity by lead with a linear attenuation coefficient of 0.567/cm. What is the shielding thickness?
Using a linear attenuation coefficient of 0.567 cm⁻¹ for lead, what thickness attenuates a photon beam to 10% of its original intensity?
Lead has a linear attenuation coefficient of 0.567 cm⁻¹. What thickness reduces beam intensity to one-tenth of its initial value?
questions.explanation:
Using the exponential attenuation law:

$$I = I_0 \, e^{-\mu x}$$

Solving for x with I/I₀ = 0.1:

$$0.1 = e^{-0.567\,x}$$

$$\ln(0.1) = -0.567\,x$$

$$x = \frac{-\ln(0.1)}{0.567} = \frac{\ln(10)}{0.567} = \frac{2.3026}{0.567} \approx \mathbf{4.06 \text{ cm}}$$

**Why the distractors are wrong:**
- **2.3 cm:** Student computes ln(10) = 2.303 but forgets to divide by μ , i.e., uses x = ln(I₀/I) without the μ term.
- **1.76 cm:** Student substitutes log₁₀ for ln: $x = \log_{10}(10)/\mu = 1/0.567 = 1.76$ cm , a common confusion between base-10 and natural logarithm.
- **1 cm:** Likely a misapplication of the HVL concept or an arbitrary round-number guess without calculation.
- **0.567 cm:** Student uses the mean free path $\bar{x} = 1/\mu = 1/0.567 \approx 1.76$ cm... or simply sets x = μ, inverting the relationship entirely.
- **0.05 cm:** Student computes x = (I/I₀)/μ = 0.1/0.567 ≈ 0.18 cm, or inverts the exponential, yielding a trivially thin and physically unreasonable result.

Reference: Bushberg et al., *The Essential Physics of Medical Imaging*, 3rd ed., Ch. 3; ICRU Report 33.

questions.correct: Using labeling, packaging, and transportation methods commensurate with the quantity, type, and hazard of radioactive materials.
questions.explanation:
The foundational philosophy of radioactive material transport safety , codified in **IAEA SSR-6 (2018)**, **49 CFR Parts 171–178**, and **IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations** , is a **graded, defense-in-depth approach**: the stringency of packaging, labeling, and transport controls is scaled proportionally to the actual radiological hazard of each shipment (activity, physical/chemical form, radionuclide type, and half-life).

This comprehensive, proportional framework is the most effective single measure because it simultaneously addresses:
- **Containment** (package performance standards scaled by activity: Excepted → Type A → Type B → Type C)
- **Communication of hazard** (White-I, Yellow-II, Yellow-III labels; transport index; UN numbers)
- **Operational controls** (segregation distances, loading limits, route restrictions for high-hazard shipments)

**Why the other options are insufficient as the primary measure:**
- **Labeling alone:** Necessary but incomplete , labels communicate hazard but do not contain it; a well-labeled deficient package is still dangerous.
- **Special vehicles:** Exclusive-use vehicles are required only for certain high-activity shipments; mandating them universally is unnecessary and economically impractical for the vast majority of low-activity medical/industrial shipments.
- **Trained personnel:** Essential but insufficient alone , without adequate packaging, even expert handlers cannot fully control exposure and contamination risks.
- **Route restrictions (bridges/tunnels):** A supplementary operational measure for the highest-hazard shipments (e.g., large Type B quantities) but does not address the underlying hazard control for the full spectrum of radioactive material transport.
- **Universal sole-use vehicles:** Overly prescriptive; IAEA SSR-6 and 49 CFR reserve exclusive-use requirements for specific high-activity thresholds, not all shipments.

Reference: IAEA SSR-6 Rev.1 (2018), §§ 100–107; 49 CFR 173.401–173.476; IATA DGR Section 10; ICRP Publication 26 (1977).

variants: At what level does loose alpha contamination become unacceptable on a radioactive materials package to be transported in a non-exclusive-use load?

questions.explanation:
Per **49 CFR 173.443(a)** and **IAEA SSR-6 Rev.1 (2018), Table I**, the limits for non-fixed (removable) surface contamination on transport packages are:

| Contaminant type | Limit |
|---|---|
| Beta/gamma emitters and low-toxicity alpha emitters | $4\,\text{Bq/cm}^2 \approx 10^{-4}\,\mu\text{Ci/cm}^2 \approx 222\,\text{dpm/cm}^2$ |
| **All other alpha emitters** | $\mathbf{0.4\,\text{Bq/cm}^2 \approx 10^{-5}\,\mu\text{Ci/cm}^2 \approx 22.2\,\text{dpm/cm}^2}$ |

Converting exactly using $1\,\mu\text{Ci} = 2{,}220{,}000\,\text{dpm}$:

$$10^{-5}\,\mu\text{Ci/cm}^2 \times 2{,}220{,}000\,\frac{\text{dpm}}{\mu\text{Ci}} = \mathbf{22.2\,\text{dpm/cm}^2}$$

Alpha emitters are held to a limit 10-fold stricter than beta/gamma emitters because alpha particles, though short-range externally, pose severe internal hazard if inhaled or ingested , and surface contamination directly threatens internal exposure via hand-to-mouth pathways.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**
- **10⁻⁴ μCi/cm² (222 dpm/cm²):** The beta/gamma non-fixed contamination limit , 10-fold too lenient for alpha emitters. A classic error of applying the beta/gamma threshold to alpha.
- **3200 dpm/cm² (1.44 × 10⁻³ μCi/cm²):** No regulatory basis; may arise from confusing the NRC surface contamination guides for unrestricted release (e.g., 3500 dpm/100 cm² = 35 dpm/cm² for alpha, from NUREG-1575 MARSSIM guidelines , itself a different context).
- **10⁻⁵ μCi total:** Omits the per-area denominator (cm²), making it a total activity value rather than an areal surface density , a fundamentally different quantity that cannot serve as a uniform package surface criterion.
- **10⁻³ μCi/cm² (2220 dpm/cm²):** 100-fold above the alpha limit; would allow dangerously contaminated packages into non-exclusive-use transport.
- **10⁻⁶ μCi/cm² (2.22 dpm/cm²):** 10-fold below the regulatory limit; an overly restrictive value that is not the established regulatory threshold.

Reference: 49 CFR 173.443(a); IAEA SSR-6 Rev.1 (2018), Table I; IATA DGR Section 10.4.2.2.

| Label | Surface dose rate | Transport index |
|---|---|---|
| White I | ≤ 0.5 mR/hr | 0 (TI = 0) |
| Yellow II | > 0.5 mR/hr and ≤ 50 mR/hr | > 0 and ≤ 1 |
| **Yellow III** | **> 50 mR/hr and ≤ 200 mR/hr** | **> 1 and ≤ 10** |

Thus Yellow III implies: surface dose rate **≤ 200 mR/hr** AND TI **≤ 10**. The **transport index** (TI) is the dose rate in mR/hr at 1 metre, and governs stacking/segregation limits in cargo environments.

**Why the other options are wrong:**
- **Surface ≤ 0.5 mR/hr:** Describes **White I** label criteria.
- **Fissile Class II, TI ≤ 0.5:** Fissile Class II labeling is a separate fissile label requirement, independent of the Yellow III activity/dose-rate label criteria.

variants: According to ICRP Publication 60, the 'equivalent dose' to a tissue is the product of the absorbed dose averaged over the tissue and:

The radiation weighting factor $w_R$ for the incident radiation type.
The applicable $w_R$ value corresponding to the radiation type and energy.

questions.explanation:
**ICRP Publication 60 (1991)** replaced the earlier concept of *dose equivalent* (which used the quality factor Q, a point function defined at a point in tissue) with the new quantity **equivalent dose** $H_T$, defined for an organ or tissue $T$:

$$H_T = \sum_R w_R \cdot D_{T,R}$$

where $D_{T,R}$ is the mean absorbed dose in tissue $T$ from radiation type $R$, and $w_R$ is the **radiation weighting factor** for that radiation type.

ICRP 60 $w_R$ values include:

| Radiation type | $w_R$ |
|---|---|
| Photons (all energies) | 1 |
| Electrons, muons | 1 |
| Protons | 5 |
| Alpha particles, fission fragments | 20 |
| Neutrons | 5–20 (energy-dependent) |

The SI unit of equivalent dose is the **sievert (Sv)**.

**Why the other options are wrong:**
- **Quality factor Q:** Used in the older ICRP 26/ICRU system to compute *dose equivalent* at a point , superseded by $w_R$ in ICRP 60. Q is a point function; $w_R$ is a radiation-field-averaged factor. The question specifically asks about ICRP 60.
- **Tissue weighting factor $w_T$:** Used in the *next* step , multiplying equivalent dose $H_T$ by $w_T$ to obtain **effective dose** $E = \sum_T w_T H_T$. It is not used to compute equivalent dose itself.
- **Nonstochastic risk coefficient:** Not a quantity in the ICRP dose calculation framework; nonstochastic (deterministic) effects use threshold-based models, not weighting coefficients.
- **Stochastic risk coefficient:** Not part of the equivalent dose definition; stochastic risk is estimated from effective dose using the detriment coefficients in ICRP 60 Annex B , a separate step downstream of equivalent dose.
- **Dose effectiveness factor / RBE / DDREF:** The DDREF modifies risk estimates from high-dose-rate data to low-dose/low-dose-rate scenarios and is not a multiplier in the equivalent dose formula.

Reference: ICRP Publication 60 (1991), §§ 2.2–2.3, Equations 2.1–2.3; ICRP Publication 103 (2007), §§ 4.3.1–4.3.2; Bushberg et al., *The Essential Physics of Medical Imaging*, 3rd ed., Ch. 23.

variants: A technician surveys a shielded pure beta-emitting source and obtains a reading of 100 mR/hr. If there is adequate shielding present to stop all beta particles, the reading is caused by:

Compton interactions of secondary photons within the shielding material.
Compton scatter events occurring as photons interact with shield electrons.
Pair production in the shield material.
Electron–positron pair production events within the shielding.
Pair production interactions of energetic photons in the shield.
Photoelectric effect in the shield material.
Photoelectric absorption interactions occurring within the shielding.
Photoelectric events in the shield producing characteristic X-rays.
Bremsstrahlung (braking radiation) produced as beta particles decelerate in the shield.
X-ray photons emitted via the bremsstrahlung process as beta particles are slowed in the shielding material.

questions.explanation:
**Bremsstrahlung** (German: *braking radiation*) is electromagnetic radiation emitted when a charged particle , here, a beta particle (electron) , undergoes Coulomb deceleration in the electric field of an atomic nucleus. The energy radiated as bremsstrahlung is given by:

$$\Delta E_{\text{brem}} \propto \frac{Z^2}{m^2} \cdot E_k$$

where $Z$ is the atomic number of the shield, $m$ is the particle mass, and $E_k$ is the kinetic energy. Key points:

- **Beta particles are fully stopped** within the shield (all ionising energy deposited), but before stopping they radiate a continuous spectrum of bremsstrahlung X-rays with energies up to $E_{\text{max}}$ of the beta spectrum.
- These **photons penetrate** the remaining shield and are detected by the survey meter, producing the 100 mR/hr reading.
- High-Z shields (e.g., lead) are deliberately **avoided** for pure beta sources precisely because their high $Z$ greatly increases bremsstrahlung yield; low-Z materials (plastic, acrylic, aluminium) are preferred.

**Why the other options are wrong:**
- **Compton scattering / Pair production / Photoelectric effect:** These are photon interaction mechanisms within shield material and are relevant to *how* the bremsstrahlung photons subsequently interact , not what *generates* the penetrating radiation in the first place.
- **Cherenkov radiation:** Cherenkov photons are optical/UV-range photons, not detectable as mR/hr on a standard ion chamber or GM survey meter; they require the particle velocity to exceed $c/n$ in the medium (possible for high-energy betas) but are not the dominant source of a dose-rate reading.
- **Characteristic X-rays from encapsulation:** While fluorescent X-rays do occur, they are discrete-energy photons from a specific element and are not the primary explanation for the broad-spectrum dose rate measurement from a beta source in a shielded configuration.

Reference: Bushberg et al., *The Essential Physics of Medical Imaging*, 3rd ed., Ch. 2; Hall & Giaccia, *Radiobiology for the Radiologist*, 8th ed.; NCRP Report No. 40.

questions.explanation:
The critical distinction here is between **stochastic effects** (which have no threshold and can occur at any dose, albeit with low probability at low doses) and **deterministic (tissue reaction) effects** (which have a dose threshold below which they do not occur):

| Effect | Classification | Threshold | Risk at chronic low-level exposure? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sterility** | Deterministic | ~150 mSv (temporary) / ~3.5–6 Sv (permanent) for gonads | ❌ No , requires doses far above chronic low-level levels |
| **Leukemia** | Stochastic | None (linear no-threshold model) | ✅ Yes |
| **Cataracts** | Historically deterministic; revised by ICRP 118 (2012) to have a **very low threshold** (~500 mGy cumulative), now effectively stochastic-like | Very low / possibly no threshold | ✅ Yes , ICRP 118 lowered the threshold to 0.5 Gy; chronic low-level exposure can accumulate to this level |
| **Skin erythema** | Deterministic | ~2 Gy acute / much higher cumulative | ❌ No , requires acutely high doses; does not occur at chronic low-level exposures |

Leukemia is a well-established stochastic risk at low doses (elevated in A-bomb survivors, radiologists in early 20th century, etc.). Cataracts are now recognised by **ICRP Publication 118 (2012)** and **NCRP Report No. 190 (2016)** as occurring at lower cumulative doses than previously thought, making them relevant to chronic occupational exposure.

**Why the other options are wrong:**
- **Sterility (I):** A deterministic effect requiring substantial doses to the gonads; does not occur from typical chronic low-level occupational or environmental exposures.
- **Skin erythema (IV):** A classic early deterministic effect of **acute** high-dose exposure (≥2 Gy); never observed from chronic low-level exposure in the occupational dose range.
- Options including sterility or skin erythema confuse deterministic threshold effects with stochastic or low-threshold risks.

Reference: ICRP Publication 60 (1991), §§ 1.3–1.4; ICRP Publication 118 (2012); Hall & Giaccia, *Radiobiology for the Radiologist*, 8th ed., Ch. 15 & 16; NCRP Report No. 190 (2016).

questions.explanation:
**450 rad (4.5 Gy)** whole-body acute exposure is close to the **LD₅₀/₆₀** , the dose lethal to 50% of an exposed population within 60 days , which for healthy adults without medical treatment is approximately **350–450 rad (3.5–4.5 Gy)** (Hall & Giaccia; UNSCEAR 1988; NCRP Report No. 138).

$$\text{LD}_{50/60} \approx 350\text{–}450\,\text{rad} \quad (\text{no medical support})$$

questions.explanation:
Charged particles traversing matter lose energy through three primary mechanisms, as described by the **Bethe–Bloch formula** and classical stopping power theory:

1. **Ionization and excitation of atomic electrons (collisional stopping power, $S_{col}$):** The dominant mechanism for heavy charged particles (protons, alpha particles) and low-to-moderate energy electrons. The charged particle transfers energy to orbital electrons via Coulomb interactions, causing ionization (electron ejection) or atomic excitation. This accounts for the majority of energy deposition.

2. **Bremsstrahlung / radiative energy loss ($S_{rad}$):** Dominant for **electrons** (low mass, $m_e$) at higher energies in high-Z materials. The ratio of radiative to collisional stopping power scales as $\approx \frac{E \cdot Z}{700}$ (E in MeV). For protons and heavier ions, bremsstrahlung is negligible due to the $1/m^2$ dependence.

3. **Nuclear interactions (spallation/inelastic nuclear reactions):** At sufficiently high energies (especially for heavy ions and protons in radiation therapy), inelastic collisions with target nuclei can cause nuclear fragmentation, ejecting secondary particles. This is the basis of the **nuclear fragmentation** problem in heavy-ion therapy.

**Why individual options are insufficient:**
- **Ionization and excitation alone (III):** The dominant mechanism but incomplete , ignores radiative and nuclear contributions.
- **Bremsstrahlung alone (II):** Only significant for electrons at high energies; not the complete picture.
- **Nuclear interactions alone (I):** Important at high energies but minor compared to collisional losses at typical therapeutic/diagnostic energies.
- **Gravitational interactions (IV):** Negligible at atomic scales; gravitational force is ~10³⁶ times weaker than the electromagnetic force relevant here.
- **Pair production (V):** A photon interaction mechanism, not a charged particle energy-loss mechanism in the classical stopping power framework.

The complete and correct answer encompasses all three physically relevant mechanisms.

Reference: Bushberg et al., *The Essential Physics of Medical Imaging*, 3rd ed., Ch. 6; Hall & Giaccia, *Radiobiology for the Radiologist*, 8th ed., Ch. 6; ICRU Report 49 (Stopping Powers for Protons and Alpha Particles).

The **linear attenuation coefficient** $\mu$ (units: cm⁻¹) quantifies the probability per unit path length that a gamma photon undergoes an interaction in a material. It depends on two independent sets of factors:

1. **Properties of the absorbing material**: density $\rho$, atomic number $Z$, and electron density , which is why $\mu$ is often normalized as the **mass attenuation coefficient** $\mu/\rho$ (cm²/g), which depends only on $Z$ and photon energy, not on the physical state or density of the material.
2. **Energy of the incident photon** $E_\gamma$: the three principal interaction cross-sections are all strongly energy-dependent:
   - **Photoelectric effect**: $\sigma_{PE} \propto Z^{4-5}/E^{3.5}$ (dominant at low energies, < ~100 keV)
   - **Compton scattering**: $\sigma_C \propto Z/E$ (dominant at intermediate energies, ~100 keV – 10 MeV)
   - **Pair production**: $\sigma_{PP} \propto Z^2 \ln E$ (threshold $E_\gamma > 1.022$ MeV; dominant at high energies)

Thus $\mu = \rho \cdot (\mu/\rho)$ where $\mu/\rho = f(Z, E_\gamma)$. Strictly speaking, **atomic number** (option 6) is also a genuine physical determinant of $\mu$. However, the question asks what $\mu$ varies with *given a specific shielding material already selected* , meaning $Z$ and $\rho$ are both fixed by that choice. The remaining independent variable across different radiation scenarios is therefore the **energy of the photon**, which is what the question is testing.

The **mass** of the shielding material (option 1) is not a fundamental determinant , a large mass of low-density foam and a small mass of dense lead can have very different $\mu$ values per unit thickness. questions.explanation:
The **W-value** (mean energy expended per ion pair formed) for air exposed to x-ray or gamma radiation is **33.7 eV/ion pair**, as established by ICRU Report 31 and widely cited in dosimetry references. This is the value used in the fundamental relationship linking exposure (in roentgens) to ionization charge:

$$X = \frac{Q}{m_{air}} \quad \text{and} \quad 1\text{ R} = 2.58 \times 10^{-4}\text{ C/kg}_{air}$$

It is critical to understand that 33.7 eV is **not** the ionization potential of air (which is ~13–16 eV for the principal constituent molecules). The W-value is higher because the total energy expended includes: (1) the ionization energy itself, (2) energy transferred to sub-ionization excitation of molecules, and (3) kinetic energy retained by secondary electrons. Option 1 (16 eV) approximates the **first ionization potential** of O₂ , not the W-value. Option 2 (32 eV) and option 3 (32.5 eV) are close but do not match the ICRU-accepted value of 33.7 eV. Option 5 (35 eV) is commonly cited for other gases (e.g., argon W ≈ 26 eV; tissue-equivalent gas W ≈ 31–35 eV) but is not the accepted air value. Option 6 (13.6 eV) is the ionization energy of hydrogen , a fundamental atomic physics constant, not a W-value. The W-value for air is essentially constant for electron energies above ~1 keV, which is why ionization chambers can be used as absolute dosimeters. Reference: ICRU Report 31 (1979); Attix, *Introduction to Radiological Physics and Radiation Dosimetry*, Ch. 12; Bushberg et al., *Essential Physics of Medical Imaging*, 3rd ed., Ch. 3.

questions.correct: Matter-antimatter annihilation producing two back-to-back 511 keV photons.
questions.explanation:
**Positron-electron annihilation** occurs when a positron ($e^+$) , after losing most of its kinetic energy through ionization interactions in matter , combines with an electron ($e^-$) at near-rest. The total rest mass energy of the two particles is converted into electromagnetic radiation:

$$e^+ + e^- \rightarrow 2\gamma \quad (E_\gamma = 511\text{ keV each})$$

The two photons are emitted **anticollinearly** (180° apart) to conserve momentum. Each photon energy equals the electron rest mass energy: $E = m_e c^2 = 0.511$ MeV. This is the physical basis of **positron emission tomography (PET)** , coincidence detection of the two 511 keV photons allows localization of the annihilation event. Compton effect (option A) involves partial energy transfer from a photon to a free/loosely-bound electron , no matter-antimatter conversion. Fusion (option C) involves combining light atomic nuclei , unrelated to electron-positron interactions. Electron fission (option D) is not a real physical process. **Pair production** (option E) is the **inverse** process: a high-energy photon ($E > 1.022$ MeV) is converted into an electron-positron pair in the Coulomb field of a nucleus , annihilation is its time-reverse. The photoelectric effect (option F) involves complete photon absorption by a bound electron. Reference: Bushberg et al., *Essential Physics of Medical Imaging*, 3rd ed., Ch. 3; Hall & Giaccia, *Radiobiology for the Radiologist*, 8th ed., Ch. 1.

questions.explanation: Two processes convert a proton to a neutron and thereby increase the neutron-to-proton ($n/p$) ratio: **electron capture** and **beta plus ($\beta^+$) decay**. The question specifically describes the conversion of a proton to a neutron via a process that *involves* the nucleus capturing a particle , this is **electron capture** (also called K-capture when the captured electron originates from the K-shell): $$p + e^- \rightarrow n + \nu_e$$ The atomic number $Z$ decreases by 1, the mass number $A$ is unchanged, and the $n/p$ ratio increases. questions.explanation: Radioactive decay is governed by quantum mechanical tunneling and nuclear force interactions at the level of individual nucleons , processes that occur within the nucleus at energy scales (MeV) vastly greater than thermal energies ($kT \approx 0.025$ eV at room temperature). Consequently, the decay constant $\lambda$ is a fixed nuclear property that is **independent of all external physical and chemical conditions**, including temperature, pressure, density, entropy, and chemical bonding state. The first-order decay law is: $$A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}, \quad t_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$ Option 1 (temperature dependence) is the most common misconception, arising from analogy with chemical reaction kinetics (Arrhenius equation), where rate constants are temperature-dependent. Options 3 and 5 (density and pressure dependence) are also incorrect for the same reason: nuclear processes are insensitive to macroscopic physical state variables. Option 4 (entropy) has no mechanistic pathway to influence nuclear decay rates. Option 6 (chemical bonding) is nearly always negligible: extremely small rate differences have been measured for electron capture nuclides (e.g., ⁷Be) in highly different chemical environments because electron capture depends on electron density at the nucleus, but these effects are unmeasurably small for all practical purposes and do not apply to alpha or beta minus decay at all. (Knoll, *Radiation Detection and Measurement*, 4th ed., Ch. 1; Attix, *Introduction to Radiological Physics and Radiation Dosimetry*, Ch. 1; ICRP Publication 107.)

questions.explanation: Gamma photons are indirectly ionizing radiation , they do not themselves carry charge, but they transfer energy to charged secondary particles that then produce ionization. There are three principal mechanisms: (1) **Photoelectric effect** , the photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron, which is ejected as a photoelectron (dominant at low energies, $E < 100$ keV in tissue); (2) **Compton scattering** , the photon transfers partial energy to a loosely bound outer-shell electron, producing a recoil (Compton) electron and a scattered photon of lower energy (dominant at diagnostic and therapeutic energies, ~100 keV to 10 MeV in tissue); (3) **Pair production** , in the Coulomb field of a nucleus, a photon with energy $\geq 1.022$ MeV is converted into an electron–positron pair, both of which ionize matter (dominant above ~10 MeV). **Bremsstrahlung** (options 2 and 3) is the production of x-rays when charged particles are decelerated , it is a consequence of the secondary electrons produced by gamma interactions, not a mechanism by which gamma photons themselves produce ionization. **Excitation** (options 4 and 5) raises orbital electrons to higher energy levels without ejecting them , it does not produce ionization. **Coherent (Rayleigh) scattering** (option 6) involves photon deflection with negligible energy transfer and produces no ionization.
